SUPERSEDED_CORRECTION: A cleaner, better-timed, verifiably-persistent repeat of this same write (patching the very first dialogue line's codes at the exact moment its buffer first populated, before any display) produced ZERO visible effect on rendering, even though the patched bytes were confirmed still present in the buffer afterward. This means the 'measurably changes what renders' claim below does not hold up -- the garbled result documented here was most likely an unrelated rendering glitch from that messier attempt's Lua runtime error/unplanned pause, not a real effect of the write itself. See MOONLIGHT_SYNDROME_FORMAT_INVESTIGATION.md's 'Correction: writing to this buffer does NOT drive rendering after all' section for the full corrected account. This record is kept for its accurate method/screenshot documentation, not for its conclusion.
claim: Writing custom character codes directly into Moonlight Syndrome's live, decompressed script buffer (found earlier this session at RAM pointer 0x801e84a4) measurably changes what the game renders on screen -- proving the buffer model (upfront-decompressed script, an offset acting as a read/display cursor rather than a write cursor) is correct. It does NOT yet produce clean, legible replacement text: the companion per-glyph position/advance-width array (found earlier at the same pointer's struct-of-arrays region) was not updated to match, producing visibly garbled/overlapping glyphs instead of the intended sentence.
method: Reset the emulator fresh, replayed input back to the same real dialogue box used throughout this investigation.

Located the not-yet-displayed 'yamete hoshii yo ne' line's 8-character code cluster ahead of the current read-cursor position (confirmed live: content well past the current display position was already present in the buffer, undecompressed-on-demand -- i.e. the whole scene's script loads upfront).

Overwrote those 8 character-code slots via GdbClient.write_memory with the confirmed codes for 'hoshii na' (ho=0x6d, shi=0x5b, i=0x51, na=0x64), repeated twice to fill all 8 slots, and read the bytes back to confirm the write landed correctly.
Advanced the dialogue via the pad bridge until the game's own read-cursor reached that exact position and rendered it live.
Captured before/after screenshots of the same script position.
result: The originally-clean 'yamete hoshii yo ne' line rendered as a small, garbled, overlapping glyph cluster instead of the intended clean 'hoshii na hoshii na' text after the patch -- a real, measurable change from the write (confirming the buffer is genuinely read live at render time, not cached/ignored), but not yet a usable, legible replacement.

screenshots.01_before_original_text.png / 01b_before: the original, unpatched line rendering cleanly, captured earlier this session before any write was made
screenshots.02_after_patched_bytes_rendered.png: full window after the patched bytes were displayed -- same script position, now garbled
screenshots.03_closeup_garbled_result.png: 6x zoomed crop isolating the garbled glyph cluster where the clean 8-character line used to render

why_the_result_is_garbled_not_clean: This game's rendering pipeline (documented earlier this session) uses a SEPARATE, parallel per-glyph position/advance-width table (found at the same pointer's struct-of-arrays block) computed from the ORIGINAL characters' pixel widths.
Only the character-code array was overwritten; the position/width array was left untouched, still describing the original 8 characters' widths.
The renderer then draws the NEW glyphs at OLD width-derived positions, producing overlapping/compressed output -- exactly the kind of artifact seen in the screenshots.
A clean injection would need to also recompute and write the position/width array to match the new glyphs' real widths, which has not been attempted yet.
earlier_negative_result_this_pass: Also tried overwriting an ALREADY-DISPLAYED line's source bytes (the very first dialogue line, already on screen) -- confirmed via screenshot this had ZERO visible effect, even after advancing to a new page below it. This is consistent with the GPU-primitive/texture-cache findings documented earlier: once a line is converted to cached sprite draw commands, it is never re-read from the source buffer, so a patch only has any effect on lines that have not yet been displayed for the first time.
conclusion: Real, live, two-sided proof: (1) the source script buffer is genuinely read at first-display time (not cached ahead of render, not ignored) -- writes to not-yet-shown lines DO change what renders; (2) a full, clean text-replacement pipeline for this game needs to handle the position/width table alongside the character codes, not just the codes alone -- a concrete, scoped next requirement, not yet built.
